catalog_quote: B. On Accent. 8. In the Congo languages the main accent falls on the initial syllable of the stem. When more than two syllables, whether radical or derivative, follow the accented syllable a secondary and weaker accent falls on the penult. ... (a) When the prefix attached to a stem consists of a nasal only, for the purposes of accent it is regarded as belonging to the syllable to which it is joined. ... (b) When in a dissyllabic word, a prefix other than the nasal takes the accent, it will be found generally that the vowel of the prefix has combined with, or been dropped before, an initial vowel of the stem. ... Note. — There are some apparent exceptions to this rule, as kulu, leg (Kongo), bato, people (Bangi). It is highly probable, however, that these were dissyllabic stems originally; in the Soko language I find ba-ito, people. (c) In a few cases the accent is shifted to mark a gram…

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation, the domain clause and the exceptions clause are all verbatim in the held archive.org text of Stapleton 1903 at Part I ch. I sec. B par. 8-9, and the book's own index confirms pp. 8-9. The secondary locator (Motingea 2004: 218 sec. 2.1.3) is a tone-and-syllable section, silent on stress, so it adds nothing to the rule but does not contradict it. (2) Deciding source: a 1903 missionary comparative handbook giving one blanket accent rule for eight 'Congo languages', Poto merely included; impressionistic, pre-tonological, examples from other languages. (3) Better sources: Glottolog's best items for Lusengo are all sketches (Glottolog's fullest description is a grammar sketch, 69 pp). Of these we hold Motingea 2004 (silent) and I downloaded Motingea 2008 from the TUFS repository (Enga de Mampoko sketch, pp. 50-51: open syllables and a few tone pairs, silent on stress). The section states only that Enga-Mampoko is an open-syllable language (V, (N)CV, (N)CSV) and, tones not having been marked in the source document, lists a few tonal minimal pairs established from external evidence (ifoku 'trou' vs ifokú 'jeune fille', etc.) plus possible metatony in the present; no mention of accent/stress anywhere in the phonology section (2.2.1-2.2.4).
